label: Concrete laboratory automation
name: Automated Concrete Testing Laboratory
title: Automated Concrete Cube Testing System | REALJET
h1:
One connected workflow.
From fresh concrete to test results.
description: REALJET integrates concrete cube preparation, curing, robotic handling and compression testing into a coordinated laboratory automation system.
intro: Concrete cube preparation, curing and compression testing, engineered as one coordinated system. REALJET plans the layout, integrates the equipment and delivers the laboratory around your workload.
alt: Concrete specimen preparation, robotic handling, curing cabinets and compression testing arranged in a coordinated laboratory

sections.heading: A laboratory that works as a system.
body: The challenge is rarely one machine. It is the handover between making a specimen, finding a curing location, retrieving it at the right age and connecting the test result to the original batch. REALJET brings those operations into one planned workflow.

points.title: Consistent preparation
points.text: Coordinate dosing, compaction, finishing and mould handling around the selected specimen method.

points.title: Organized curing
points.text: Connect specimen identity, available storage positions and testing ages.

points.title: Connected testing
points.text: Bring handling, compression testing and records into a coordinated test sequence.

sections.heading: Follow the specimen. Close the mould cycle.
body: From a defined collection point, fresh concrete moves to the preparation cell. Filled moulds enter initial storage; specimens are demoulded, identified and transferred to curing. At the scheduled age, the handling system delivers them to the testing workstation.
sections.alt: Overall concrete laboratory configuration with preparation, curing storage, transfer and elevated feeding
sections.caption: Preparation, curing and testing planned around a shared material flow.

sections.heading: Six modules. A configuration for your laboratory.
body: Build a new laboratory or focus on the operation that consumes the most time. REALJET coordinates the mechanical, electrical and data interfaces between the selected modules.

sections.heading: Start with your operation, not a fixed equipment list.
body: A ready-mix producer may need automatic preparation close to the batching plant. A testing center may receive already-cast specimens and start with storage and compression testing. A precast factory needs a clear link between production batches and laboratory records.

sections.heading: Engineering from layout to commissioning.
body: REALJET leads the project through scope definition, layout development, equipment integration, installation and commissioning. The project specification records the responsibilities, operating conditions and acceptance checks before equipment is finalized.

steps.title: Define the workload
steps.text: Record daily and peak intake, specimen geometry, test ages and existing equipment.

steps.title: Plan the configuration
steps.text: Balance preparation capacity, curing inventory, transport and testing demand.

steps.title: Verify the interfaces
steps.text: Confirm collection points, machine signals, software, utilities and access.

steps.title: Install and hand over
steps.text: Commission the agreed sequence, train operators and prepare maintenance and recovery procedures.

sections.heading: Specify the laboratory around measurable inputs.
body: Use consistent units across every part of the project. Specimens per hour describe preparation or testing; storage capacity describes specimens held at the same time. A group count also needs the number of specimens in each group.

rows: Geometry, dimensions, group size and concrete types
Daily intake, peak periods, preparation and testing shifts
Required methods, test ages, retained samples and available positions
Pressure machines, moulds, storage and laboratory software
Floor plan, access, water, drainage, compressed air and electrical supply
Operating sequence, specimen tracking, environmental checks and test interfaces

faq: Can we automate only part of our laboratory?
Yes. REALJET can scope a preparation cell, a curing and handling arrangement, or a robotic testing workstation. The interfaces are planned so the selected module fits the existing operation.
Do we need to replace our pressure testing machines?
Not necessarily. Send the machine make, model, controller and available interface information. REALJET reviews how loading, guarding, test control and data exchange can be coordinated.
How is curing capacity determined?
Start with daily specimen intake and split it by test age. Calculate how long each group remains in storage, then allow for retained specimens, operating peaks and usable positions.
Does the system cover cylinders or cores?
The cube configuration is the starting point for this solution. Cylinder and core requirements need a separate review of gripping, preparation, curing and compression testing.
Who coordinates the complete project?
REALJET is the solution delivery and integration lead, coordinating the selected equipment, controls, site interfaces and commissioning scope.

body: After the initial curing period, the demoulding station separates the specimen from the mould. The mould returns through cleaning and release-agent preparation; the selected mould design can include a bottom-paper station.

body: Cleaning is part of the operating cycle. Collection trays, wash points and drainage routes need to remain accessible when the cell is operating. REALJET also plans access for nozzle, feeder and gripping-tool maintenance.

faq: Is demoulding included?
The preparation scope can include initial storage, demoulding and mould recycling. The agreed equipment list identifies which stations are included.
How many cubes can the machine make?
Capacity is specified for the selected mould, concrete, preparation sequence and operating shift. Send the daily and peak specimen workload so the cell can be sized correctly.
Can the cell handle different concrete mixes?
The material review covers workability, aggregate size, setting behavior and the required cleaning between batches. Special mixes need a defined validation sequence.
Does it include the fresh concrete supply line?
Supply can be local or connected through a separate feeding and transfer module. The collection point, transfer time and interface are agreed with the preparation layout.

faq: Can we use our existing curing room?
REALJET reviews the room, storage positions, environment, access and handling route to determine what can be retained.
Does the cabinet include automated loading?
Environmental control and specimen handling are separate scope items. They can be combined, with the selected loading mechanism shown in the configuration.
Is one temperature and humidity setting suitable for every market?
The project method determines the required conditions. The configuration is specified for that method rather than a universal setting.
How do we size the system?
Provide daily specimen intake, group size, test ages, retained samples and peak workload. These inputs define the occupied inventory and usable storage requirement.

This can be evaluated against reach, guarding, test-cycle duration and access. The layout and handling schedule determine the practical arrangement.
Is dimensional measurement included?
It is a configurable workstation function. The quotation defines the measuring equipment, calibration and connection to the test record.
Can the workstation test cylinders or cores?
Those specimens need a separate handling and method review, including end preparation and gripping. They are not assumed to be covered by the cube configuration.
Who issues the test report?
The workstation supplies the agreed test records. Report review, approval and release remain part of the laboratory's quality process.

label: Cost & capacity guide
name: Concrete Laboratory Automation Cost & ROI
title: Concrete Lab Automation Cost & ROI Guide | REALJET
h1:
What determines the cost
of laboratory automation?
description: Understand concrete laboratory automation cost, curing capacity, maintenance and ROI before requesting a project-specific REALJET proposal.
intro: Start with the work the system must perform. Preparation workload, curing inventory, existing equipment and site interfaces shape both the investment and the operating return.
alt: Concrete laboratory floor plan used for scope and capacity evaluation

sections.heading: Define the scope before comparing prices.
body: A preparation cell, a robot-fed pressure machine and an integrated laboratory are different purchases. Compare the same operations, utilities, interfaces and handover responsibilities before comparing equipment prices.

sections.heading: Include the costs around the machines.
body: The initial investment can include tooling, moulds, controls, transport, installation, site works, software interfaces and commissioning. Ongoing cost includes energy, water, cleaning materials, wear parts, maintenance and software support.

rows: Which preparation, curing, handling and testing operations are included?
Which existing machines and software need interfaces?
What power, water, drainage, access or structure is required?
What checks, training and method verification are included?
What cleaning, wear parts, maintenance and support will be needed?

sections.heading: Calculate inventory from the age profile.
body: For each specimen group, multiply its daily intake by the number of days it occupies storage, then add the groups together. Allow separately for retained specimens, access and peaks. The capacity calculator below uses one storage period as a starting scenario.

sections.heading: Use net operating savings, not a headline labor percentage.
body: Annual net benefit is the labor cost actually removed or avoided, plus verified extra contribution or reduced rework, less added operating and maintenance cost. Static payback divides initial investment by that annual net benefit.
sections.note: Calculation example only, not a REALJET price or promised return. It excludes finance, tax and the time value of money.

sections.heading: A phased project may be the better first investment.
body: If the workload is small, methods vary frequently or the available operating period is short, assess a single module or an instrument upgrade. The first project should address an identifiable bottleneck and leave a clear route for expansion.

sections.heading: Prepare an estimate that can become a project.
body: Send daily and peak specimens, dimensions, group size, test ages, the laboratory plan and existing machines. REALJET uses these inputs to define an equipment and integration scope rather than quoting an unspecified complete line.

faq: Why is there no single price for the complete system?
Storage capacity, preparation operations, machines retained and site interfaces vary between laboratories. A defined scope makes the estimate comparable and useful.
Does a faster robot guarantee more reports per day?
No. Preparation, curing schedules, machine cycles, cleaning and report review can each limit output.
Can a small laboratory start with one module?
A phased project can focus on its largest repeatable task. The investment review should include the cost of integration and the actual work saved.

label: Equipment selection guide
name: Manual vs Automated Concrete Cube Testing
title: Manual vs Automated Concrete Cube Testing | REALJET
h1:
Choose the right level
of laboratory automation.
description: Compare manual handling, automatic compression machines and integrated robotic concrete laboratories with REALJET's practical selection guide.
intro: Automation can control a test cycle, move a specimen or coordinate the entire laboratory. The right choice depends on where time is spent and how repeatable the workload is.
alt: Robot positioned beside concrete testing stations

sections.heading: Separate automatic testing from automatic handling.
body: An automatic compression machine controls the test sequence. Operators may still identify, measure, load and remove the specimen. A robot-fed workstation adds those handling steps; laboratory integration connects preparation and curing as well.

sections.heading: Compare the operations, not the label.
body: Ask who performs each task and what happens when the normal sequence fails. This exposes the useful difference between an automatic machine and an integrated laboratory.

sections.heading: Choose the first module around a measurable bottleneck.
body: If mould preparation consumes the shift, begin with preparation. If staff spend time finding and carrying stored cubes, examine curing access and transfer. If machine loading dominates a repetitive test queue, review a robotic workstation.

sections.heading: Keep maintenance in the comparison.
body: Automatic handling adds gripping tools, position sensors, interfaces and safety systems. Include access, cleaning, wear and recovery in the operating plan. More equipment is valuable only when the workload and service arrangement justify it.

sections.heading: Use a staged path when conditions are still changing.
body: Retain suitable instruments, automate one repeatable operation and preserve the specimen identity across handovers. Add modules when the next bottleneck is understood. REALJET can compare the layout and interfaces for both the first stage and later expansion.

faq: Does automatic mean no people are needed?
No. Even a connected system needs material replenishment, checks, maintenance, exception handling and technical oversight.
Should we replace working instruments first?
Not necessarily. Review their physical access, controller and data interface before deciding whether to retain, upgrade or replace them.
Is a complete system always the best option?
No. Workload, operating life, repeatability, available space and maintenance support should determine the useful scope.

label: Technical selection guide
name: Specimen Types, Curing & Method Adaptation
title: Concrete Specimens & Lab Automation Methods | REALJET
h1:
The specimen and method
come before the machinery.
description: Plan concrete laboratory automation around cube, cylinder and core geometry, curing methods, testing equipment and laboratory validation.
intro: Geometry, curing and the selected test method affect every part of laboratory automation. Define them before choosing moulds, grippers, storage and compression equipment.
alt: Concrete cube placed on a compression machine platen

sections.heading: Cube, cylinder and core are different workflows.
body: A 150 mm cube is the starting geometry for this solution. Cylinders and drilled cores introduce different gripping, end preparation, dimensional measurement and test requirements. They need their own engineering review rather than a report-template change.

sections.heading: Map the method to the operation.
body: The standards below identify subjects to review during specification. The applicable edition, project specification and laboratory method determine the final procedure; this guide does not replace those documents.

heads: Subject to map into the workflow
rows: Making and curing specimens for strength tests
Making and curing concrete test specimens in the field
Compression testing of cylindrical concrete specimens
Mixing rooms, moist storage and water storage facilities

sections.heading: Select the curing path for its purpose.
body: Standard curing, field-related curing and temperature-matched arrangements do not serve identical purposes. The selected environment, storage period and test age must remain connected to the specimen record. Special curing functions require a defined equipment scope.

sections.heading: Validate more than the robot position.
body: Verification covers mould condition, preparation sequence, environmental distribution, machine calibration, specimen placement and records. A correct robot movement alone does not validate a material test.

points.title: Equipment checks
points.text: Force measurement, sensing, access and environment.

points.title: Workflow checks
points.text: Identification, handover, exception handling and recovery.

points.title: Record checks
points.text: Original readings, calculated results, user actions and exports.

sections.heading: Laboratory competence remains a separate requirement.
body: ISO/IEC 17025 concerns the competence of testing and calibration laboratories. Installing automated equipment does not automatically provide laboratory accreditation. The laboratory reviews method validation, calibration, records and the effect on its recognized scope.

sections.heading: Bring the method into the first discussion.
body: Send the project location, applicable methods, specimen sizes, test ages, curing requirements and existing instruments. REALJET uses these inputs to define the equipment adaptation and acceptance checks.

faq: Does one cube configuration meet every national method?
No. The project must define its actual specimen, preparation, curing and test procedure. The equipment is specified around that definition.
Is high humidity at 20°C a universal curing requirement?
No. The selected method and project procedure determine the required environment and its monitoring.
Who reviews the laboratory's accreditation impact?
The laboratory's technical and quality team works with its relevant accreditation or approval body. Equipment scope and method acceptance should be reviewed together.
